read.title: Arrows that push electrons
text: Most organic reactions are polar: an electron-rich nucleophile donates a pair of electrons to an electron-poor electrophile. Chemists show this with curved arrows. Each arrow starts at a lone pair or a bond, the electrons that move, and ends at the atom that receives them. A fishhook arrow, with half a head, moves a single electron and is used for radical reactions.

Consider HBr adding to ethylene. The C=C π bond is electron-rich, so it acts as the nucleophile and attacks the hydrogen of HBr, pushing the H–Br electrons onto bromine. The result is a carbocation intermediate and a bromide ion. In a second step bromide, now the nucleophile, attacks the positively charged carbon to give bromoethane.

An energy diagram tracks such a reaction. Each step passes over a transition state, a fleeting energy maximum, and the carbocation sits in a valley between them as an intermediate. The highest barrier sets the rate. By the Hammond postulate, an uphill step has a transition state that looks like the high-energy carbocation, so anything that stabilizes the cation, such as extra alkyl groups, also speeds the step. That idea explains a great deal of the selectivity you will see in later chapters.
